 South Dakota State football aiming to stop SIU’s late surge in regular season road finale
 Nov 10, 2026 
 — 
 By Gavin Struve | The Brookings Register 
 in SDSU Jackrabbits , Sports 
 Southern Illinois is the lone conference foe that SDSU didn’t face in head coach Dan Jackson’s first season leading the Jackrabbits. 
 After passing a road test with flying colors at Northern Iowa this past weekend, South Dakota State’s football team has its last away game of the regular season (and perhaps its last of the rest of the season altogether depending on its FCS playoff seeding).
 The Jackrabbits are visiting Southern Illinois, who started the season ranked No. 16 nationally coming off a 7-5 season. As high as the Salukis were ranked, they were still sixth in the Missouri Valley Football Conference (MVFC) preseason poll. That’s precisely where they are in the league standings right now at 5-5 overall and 3-3 in conference. They may be rounding into form ahead of Saturday’s 1 p.m. game.
 “When you have really good coaches, which they do, your team gets better throughout the season,” SDSU head coach Dan Jackson said. “It should be (getting better). And that’s what I’ve always noticed with Southern Illinois is they get better as the season goes on, and this year’s no different. They look pretty good to me.”
 Jackson noted that it’s both SIU’s senior day and a chance to make a playoff push, so the Salukis have plenty to play for.
 SIU started the season with a loss to West Florida, a first-year NCAA Division I program, but star quarterback DJ Williams got injured early in that game. The Salukis’ other defeats are understandable, too. They lost at Illinois and to Youngstown State, South Dakota and Illinois State.
 The Salukis weren’t particularly competitive against any of those teams, but they’ve taken care of business against the teams they’ve been expected to beat. They defeated Northern Iowa and Indiana State over the past two games, with a bye week in between, and Williams has looked increasingly healthy and dynamic the further removed he is from suffering the knee injury.
 “DJ’s his own challenge,” Jackson said. “He’s big. He’s big like Chase (Mason), but he runs like Beau (Walter Payton Award winner Beau Brungard) and has an arm like Chase. He’s a very good player, so we’re going to need to do some things differently.”
 Williams threw for 2,846 yards and 22 touchdowns compared to five interceptions last season, while rushing for 847 yards and 18 touchdowns on 5.8 yards per carry. The injury has made him less effective as a runner this season, but he still has rushed for eight touchdowns while throwing for 10 touchdowns compared to four interceptions across eight full games this fall.
 The Salukis will need Williams’ dual-threat ability to make a dent in SDSU’s eighth-ranked rush defense. The Jackrabbits haven’t faced a running quarterback in a few weeks.
 Williams rushed for 89 yards and two touchdowns against Northern Iowa and threw for 211 yards, four touchdowns and no interceptions against Indiana State.
 “DJ’s healthy,” Jackson said. “Their quarterback has not been healthy all season. He got hurt in their first game, missed one game and then you could tell he was just really toughing it out. And he just wasn’t moving around. And now I’ve watched their last two games, he’s very dynamic. So if they call a pass play and it’s not there, he’s tucking it and running it and he looks very, very explosive, like one of the better athletes in the conference type of explosive.”
 SIU now has a quarterback run game element that it didn’t for much of the season, and Jackson thinks it’s leading to the Salukis’ other skill players making more plays.
 Senior receiver Kyle Thomas has emerged as the Salukis’ top offensive weapon. After recording just 10 receiving yards last season, Thomas has caught 45 passes for 694 yards (fourth in the MVFC) and eight touchdowns (third in the MVFC).
 SDSU’s defense is contending with some injuries that could make containing Williams and Thomas even tougher. Senior safety Dontay Johnson, the leader of SDSU’s secondary, “has a shot to be back this weekend,” according to Jackson. Another starter, junior cornerback Paul Kim, is going to attempt to play. Redshirt sophomore defensive tackle Rhett Schaefer is hurt, too.
 Nonetheless, Jackson said SDSU’s roster is built with depth in mind. It can weather a storm. The recipe for an upset may instead come from SIU’s defense rather than its offense.
 SIU’s defense is more forgiving than SDSU’s. The Salukis rank 52nd in pass yards allowed per game and 51st in rush yards allowed per game, but they’re disruptive, which can lead to some variability.
 The Salukis rank fourth nationally in interceptions, with 13 this season. SIU is also in the top third nationally in sacks, and much of that production has come from two players.
 Senior defensive end Ibrahim Sanogo is second in the MVFC with 7.5 sacks, and senior cornerback Sebastian Vargas leads the MVFC with four interceptions.
 “Their secondary has some very talented athletes in it, especially at corner,” Jackson said. “I think those guys have been playmakers for them.”
 This is the one MVFC team that SDSU didn’t play last year, so the Jackrabbits don’t have film from a 2025 game to go back and watch. Instead, the ‘Jacks are going back and watching all the games that SIU head coach Nick Hill has coached against them.
 That’s not all SDSU is doing differently. Jackson hasn’t coached against the Salukis yet, but he’s made the trip to Carbondale, Illinois, before as an assistant.
 He thought the Jackrabbits could do the trip better than they have in the past, so they adjusted the time they’re flying Friday and are staying closer to the stadium now. It’s all in an effort to keep their three-game winning streak rolling heading into the regular season finale and to stop the Salukis from getting hot late.
